problem: State-of-the-art VLN agents (Seq2Seq, Speaker-Follower, RCM, Regretful, FAST) do not generalize from the path lengths they were trained on to other lengths. Agents trained on R4R lose a lot of path fidelity (SDTW) on longer tasks (R6R/R8R) and even on shorter ones (R2R). The paper frames this as length generalization: can an agent learn from short instructions and still follow much longer ones?
motivation: Collecting and training on long annotated instruction–trajectory pairs is costly, while humans extrapolate from short navigation experiences. The authors' Fig. 1 finding drives the paper: agents trained on R4R fall well below in-domain agents on every other length. Optimizing a fidelity reward (RCM(fidelity)) helps but is not enough to transfer.
key_idea: Decompose a long instruction into short sub-instructions (BabySteps) and execute them one after another. Past BabySteps are summarized by a forgetting-weighted memory. Training is two-phase: imitation learning on individual BabySteps, then curriculum RL that trains on increasingly many consecutive BabySteps.
insight: Length generalization comes from three pieces, each shown by an ablation. (1) Hierarchical memory that down-weights older BabySteps: without memory, SDTW is 9.9 (in-domain) / 9.6 (others); with an LSTM summary 14.4/14.3; plain averaging (γ=0) 15.1/14.4; exponential forgetting with γ=0.5 17.3/17.5. (2) Curriculum RL: IL alone gives 11.1 SDTW, IL+direct RL 13.6, and CRL rises lecture by lecture to 17.3 (4th lecture), so warm-starting from short sub-tasks lets RL handle long horizons. (3) Template-based BabyStep segmentation beats sentence-wise splitting (avg SDTW 18.4 vs 15.4). Fidelity-oriented training trades SR/SPL for instruction following: FAST still wins in-domain SR, and RCM(goal) wins SPL on long datasets because it takes shortcuts.
method: BabyStep identification: heuristic, template-based chunking of instructions. Sentences are split on periods; SpaCy POS tagging chunks noun and verb phrases; noun/verb blacklists yield landmark words; non-actionable sentences and stop-condition sentences are merged into their neighbours. The same procedure is applied at test time, so no oracle segmentation is needed.

Trajectory–BabyStep alignment without extra annotation: a weakly supervised multi-label landmark classifier is trained on trajectories. It is a 2-layer CNN over the 6×6 ResNet-152 panorama features plus an MLP, with max-pooling over states and BCE against the landmarks mentioned in the instruction. Dynamic programming then segments expert trajectories to maximize landmark-score agreement with each BabyStep.

Memory buffer / context: z_m = MLP(sum of past BabyStep instruction encodings, sum of past BabyStep trajectory encodings). The encodings are hierarchical, one per BabyStep: an LSTM for instructions; for trajectories, two Bi-LSTMs over actions and states whose outputs are concatenated. Weights follow exponential forgetting, α_i ∝ exp(−γ(m−1−i)) with γ=0.5.

Policy: Speaker-Follower-style LSTM (hidden size 512) with visual attention over 36 panoramic views and text attention over the current BabyStep encoding u(x_m). The attended text is concatenated with the context z_m, passed through a 2-layer MLP, and dot-producted with navigable-direction embeddings. The action space is panoramic nav-graph.

Phase 1, imitation learning: student-forcing IL on each BabyStep independently. For each BabyStep the agent is preset to the expert's last state and given the expert-history context. This runs 50k iterations.

Phase 2, curriculum RL: warm-started from IL, policy gradient with a terminal reward of SR + CLS (fidelity-oriented). In lecture k, the agent is placed at the expert state before the (M−k+1)th BabyStep and must execute the last k BabySteps itself. There are 4 lectures of 10k iterations each; the best-SDTW model is carried to the next lecture.

setting.backbone: LSTM encoder–decoder policy with cross-modal attention (Speaker-Follower style) over frozen ImageNet ResNet-152 features, plus LSTM/Bi-LSTM instruction and trajectory encoders with GloVe embeddings; trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Main models trained on the R4R train split (233,532 instructions). Variants are also trained on R2R (14,039), R6R (89,632) and R8R (94,731); R6R/R8R are new datasets built by concatenating R2R trajectories 3× / 4×. The '+' variants are additionally pre-trained with Speaker-Follower speaker-generated data augmentation. BabyStep segmentation and alignments come from heuristics plus a weakly supervised landmark classifier (no extra human annotation).
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (ResNet-152 features of 36 views, 12 headings × 3 elevations, plus orientation features)
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (panoramic action space of Fried et al.); max 10 steps per BabyStep
setting.privileged: none. At test time the instruction is segmented into BabySteps by the heuristic segmenter; no oracle sub-trajectories are used.

numbers_note: The paper's 'PL' (path length) is mapped to TL. R6R and R8R are new datasets introduced by the paper, evaluated on val-unseen splits built from concatenated R2R val-unseen paths. The appendix also has transfer results for R6R- and R8R-trained models on other lengths; those are not all listed here. Figures 1 and 4 (per-length curves) are plots only. All baselines were re-run or reimplemented by the authors; the sanity check against reported R2R numbers is in the appendix. No R2R test-server results are reported.
results: Trained on R4R, BabyWalk+ leads every baseline on path fidelity in-domain: CLS 49.4 / SDTW 17.3 vs RCM(fidelity) 39.2/13.7 and FAST 34.0/15.5. FAST still has the higher in-domain SR (36.2 vs 29.6 for BabyWalk). The out-of-domain gains are larger: averaged over R2R/R6R/R8R, BabyWalk+ reaches CLS 47.9 / SDTW 17.5 vs the best baselines at 35.7 CLS (RCM(fidelity)) and 10.9 SDTW (RCM(goal)). On R6R/R8R its SDTW (13.6/11.1) is roughly double FAST's (7.7/6.3). Trained on R2R, BabyWalk+ reaches 43.8 SR / 36.9 SDTW in-domain and transfers to R6R/R8R almost as well as the R4R-trained model.
limitations: BabyStep segmentation is heuristic (POS templates, blacklists) and the trajectory alignment is only weakly supervised. Segmentation is noisy, e.g. on R4R it ignores the natural boundaries between the two concatenated paths; the authors suggest this may explain why R4R→R2R transfer is weaker than R2R→R4R.
Gains are in fidelity metrics (CLS/nDTW/SDTW), not goal-reaching. SR is below FAST in-domain, and SPL on long tasks is low (e.g. 7.4 on R8R), below RCM(goal).
The gap between short and long tasks remains large. Evaluation covers only discrete nav-graph Matterport3D environments with R2R-derived synthetic long instructions (R6R/R8R are concatenations).
